title: C++ Idioms and Design Patterns
summary: **Idioms** are solutions specific to C++: RAII, pImpl, copy and swap, the Rule of Zero, CRTP, type erasure. **Design patterns** are recipes that apply in any language: Strategy, Observer, Factory, Visitor. Knowing their names lets you design faster and talk to other programmers.
ideas:
1. Convert one of your classes to pImpl. Change a private member and observe which files recompile.
2. Implement a game character's behaviour with the State pattern twice: with virtual classes, and with `std::variant`.
3. Build a factory registry in which shapes register themselves through static objects.

cards.q: Why must the destructor of a pImpl class be defined in the source file?
cards.a:
Deleting `Impl` needs its full definition, found only there

Defining the destructor (even as `= default`) in the `.cpp`, after `Impl` is defined, lets `unique_ptr` delete it.

cards.q: What is the modern C++ alternative to the classic Visitor pattern?
cards.a:
`std::variant` with `std::visit`

A variant of the node types plus `std::visit` handles each type, with the compiler checking every case is covered.

cards.q: What are the costs of pImpl?
cards.a:
A heap allocation per object and an extra indirection

In exchange you get a stable header and faster rebuilds, since private changes no longer recompile users.

It is a global in disguise that hides dependencies

Code that reaches for `Logger::instance()` hides that it needs a logger. Passing the dependency in makes it visible and replaceable.
